text: Foton-M No.4 is a Russian microgravity and bioscience research spacecraft launched in July 2014 as part of the Foton programme. It is the fourth spacecraft in the Foton-M series and the first to use the 34KSM configuration, which incorporates the equipment module from a Yantar satellite instead of the Zenit module used on previous missions. The spacecraft was launched from the Baikonur Cosmodrome on 18 July 2014 using a Soyuz-2-1a carrier rocket. The launch was successful, with the satellite separating from the rocket and initiating data transmission to ground controllers. However, after completing four orbits, it stopped responding to ground commands, preventing it from performing a scheduled orbit-raising maneuver. Satellite control was restored on 26 July, by which time some microgravity experiments had already begun. On 1 August, Oleg Ostapenko, head of Roskosmos, stated that the satellite would proceed with its original two-month mission plan despite the canceled orbit-boosting maneuver. All experiments were completed by 27 August, and Roskosmos decided to return the spacecraft to Earth on 1 September, two weeks earlier than the originally planned landing date of 15 September. The payload included specimens for studying the biological effects of zero gravity and cosmic radiation, such as geckos, silkworm eggs, dried seeds, fruit flies, and mushrooms. The geckos were part of a biology experiment by Russia's Institute of Medico-Biological Problems to examine the effects of weightlessness on mating; initial reports after the payload's return indicated that all five geckos launched in the experiment had died, and an investigation into the cause of death is ongoing. In contrast, the fruit flies survived the mission and successfully bred and developed. Another experiment aimed to assess the impact of microgravity on semiconductor crystal growth, with the goal of producing higher-quality crystals for electronics applications.
